name: CNN patch classifier on shoreline patches

identity.method_name: CNN patch classifier (binary image classification, e.g. a small from-scratch CNN or a lightly transfer-learned ResNet18/MobileNet backbone) on shoreline patches
identity.core_idea: Sample small fixed-size multi-band image patches centred on points spaced along each lake's buffer ring (the OpenStreetMap-derived shoreline), for each available year. Feed each patch through a CNN that outputs a single binary label -- encroached or not-encroached -- rather than a per-pixel mask. This is the standard 'deep baseline' framing: patch-level image classification, trained with cross-entropy on whatever labels can be obtained, is the simplest deep-learning approach any more sophisticated segmentation or change-detection model must be shown to beat.
identity.official_dataset_ids: None. This method is built entirely from the project's own cached Sentinel-2 bands (B02, B03, B04, B08, B11, SCL, 20 m EPSG:32643) and the OpenStreetMap lake-boundary multipolygon; no external official dataset ID applies. If a transfer-learning backbone is used, its pretraining source is ImageNet-1k (not a geospatial dataset ID, and not resolution- or band-compatible with Sentinel-2).

fit_to_project.ground_truth_proxy_strategy: This is the organising problem for this entire item. The only two honest options are: (a) manual annotation -- a student visually judges each shoreline patch, per lake per year, as 'encroached' or 'not' using higher-resolution reference imagery (Google Earth Pro historical imagery, Bhuvan, ESRI World Imagery), since no authoritative encroached/not-encroached list exists (KTCDA and BBMP records are not digitised or accessible per item B2); or (b) programmatic weak supervision, reusing the project's own MNDWI/NDVI/OSM-building-overlap rules as noisy labelling functions. Option (b) is circular: it trains the CNN to imitate the very classical rule it is supposed to be compared against, so any 'CNN beats the baseline' claim built on those labels is not defensible. Option (a) is the only genuinely independent source, and it costs real student time (estimated below, roughly 6-10 student-days dominated by labelling, not modelling).
fit_to_project.input_required: Multi-band Sentinel-2 raster patches along each lake's shoreline buffer (already available) plus a binary encroachment label per patch per year (not available; must be created, see above). No additional imagery acquisition is needed, only labelling effort.
fit_to_project.viable_with_42_rows: only-if-reframed. The method is per-patch, not per-lake-year: sampling points every ~20-40 m around a lake perimeter of a few kilometres, across 6 lakes and 7 years, could nominally yield several thousand patch-year samples. But this is a reframing, not a real increase in independent information -- patches along the same shoreline in the same year are strongly spatially autocorrelated, and the same physical location revisited across 7 years is strongly temporally autocorrelated. The effective independent sample size for any honest test is much closer to 6 (the number of distinct lakes) than to the thousands of raw patches, since a hold-out that is not lake-based leaks.
fit_to_project.viable_without_ground_truth: needs-weak-labels. See ground_truth_proxy_strategy: the model cannot be trained at all without either manually created labels or the circular MNDWI/NDVI-derived proxy.
fit_to_project.resolution_match_20m: Patch classification is native to the project's existing 20 m grid in the sense that no foreign checkpoint resolution is being imported, but there is a real, project-specific mismatch between the legal buffer widths being tested and the pixel size: a 30 m buffer (the Supreme-Court-reinstated Bengaluru Master Plan distance) is only 1.5 pixels wide at 20 m, and the quashed 75 m NGT buffer is under 4 pixels wide. A patch large enough to give the CNN useful spatial context (e.g. 5x5 or 7x7 pixels, i.e. 100-140 m across) necessarily mixes open water, buffer, and land well beyond the buffer itself, so the model is being asked to classify a much coarser strip of ambiguous mixed land cover than the legal boundary it is meant to speak to.
fit_to_project.label_source_needed: Manual visual annotation by the student/team using historical high-resolution reference imagery (Google Earth Pro, Bhuvan, ESRI World Imagery) is the only non-circular source. No authoritative encroachment label source exists for these lakes (see project_constraints.ground_truth and item B2).
fit_to_project.fixes_which_stated_limitation: None directly. It does not add a new time-varying data source (so it does not fix limitation 2), and it does not itself resolve limitation 3 (no ground truth) -- it only prices out the cost of manufacturing some weak labels, which is a useful contribution but not a fix. It offers only a superficial reframing of limitation 1 (42 rows), since the resulting patch-level sample is not made up of independent observations (see viable_with_42_rows). It does nothing for limitation 4 (dry-season-only scenes).
fit_to_project.handles_desilting_confound: Only as well as its label source does. If labels come from the MNDWI/NDVI proxy, desilting years will be mislabelled the same way the current method already mislabels them (indistinguishable from encroachment). If labels come from careful manual annotation with annotators specifically trained to recognise a drained-for-maintenance lakebed (dry, bare, temporary) versus a genuinely built-up former lakebed, the CNN could in principle be taught the distinction -- but this depends entirely on the labelling protocol, not on any property of the CNN architecture itself, and is a real annotation-design burden on top of the labelling cost already estimated.
fit_to_project.handles_hyacinth_confound: Not automatically. A CNN given only reflectance patches has no inherent way to separate a dense water-hyacinth mat from informal cultivation or vegetated encroachment -- both appear as green, vegetated pixels in true or false colour. Annotators would need to consult the published macrophyte-cover mapping for Bellandur and Varthur (MDPI Remote Sensing 2020, DOI 10.3390/rs12223843) while labelling, and even then the CNN itself, trained on raw bands, may not learn to make this distinction reliably from only 6 lakes' worth of examples.
fit_to_project.legal_traceability: Patches are sampled from the OpenStreetMap proxy shoreline/buffer only; the CNN's output has no independent link to Karnataka Tank Conservation and Development Authority records, Survey of India records, Bhuvan, or the National Wetland Atlas 2024. Whichever buffer distance is tested (30 m reinstated Master Plan buffer, or the quashed 75 m NGT buffer, per item B1) is applied only as a sampling geometry around the non-statutory OSM polygon, exactly the same limitation the current classical method already carries.
fit_to_project.temporal_granularity: Patches are drawn once per available Sentinel-2 scene per year, so the label and the imagery both do vary year to year in principle -- but each year is represented by a single dry-season-minimum composite (limitation 4), so the 'temporal' signal the CNN sees is 7 single snapshots, not a real intra-annual trajectory, and any within-year variability (e.g. transient hyacinth bloom timing) is invisible to it.

implementation.libraries: PyTorch or TensorFlow/Keras; torchvision for an optional ResNet18/MobileNetV2 transfer-learning backbone; scikit-learn for splitting, metrics and calibration; rasterio/rioxarray for patch extraction from the existing Sentinel-2 stack.
implementation.pretrained_weights: ImageNet-pretrained backbones (ResNet, EfficientNet, MobileNet) are widely available (torchvision, timm) but were trained on 3-channel, 8-bit, 224x224 natural images -- not 5-band, 16-bit reflectance patches at 20 m -- so their transfer value here is limited and unverified; a small from-scratch CNN (a handful of 3x3 conv blocks, global average pooling, a dense layer, on the order of 50,000-150,000 parameters, sized the way the project's own reference architecture for a comparable-scale problem was sized) is the more defensible choice given the tiny number of true training examples available.
implementation.licence: Fully open. Self-built model using standard open-source libraries (PyTorch/TensorFlow, both permissively licensed); no third-party weights, data or code licence issues.
implementation.compute_requirement: Trivial. A small CNN over 5-band, 20 m patches at this data scale (at most a few thousand patches) trains in minutes on a laptop CPU, and comfortably within free Colab/Kaggle GPU limits if used at all. This is the cheapest deep-learning item on the whole list from a pure compute standpoint.
implementation.student_days: Model code and training: 1-2 days. The real cost is labelling, which is the bottleneck the note asks to be stated honestly: defining the patch-sampling scheme (0.5 day); manually annotating a usable set of patches across 6 lakes x 7 years using historical high-resolution reference imagery, realistically at least 150-300+ labelled patch-years for a workable train/leave-one-lake-out-test split, at a rate of roughly 40-80 judgements per hour once a protocol is set (3-6 student-days); plus a second annotator pass and Cohen's kappa cross-check for inter-annotator agreement (1-2 days). Honest total: roughly 6-10 student-days, most of it labelling rather than modelling.

evaluation.metrics: Precision, recall and F1 for the encroached class specifically, plus ROC-AUC and a full confusion matrix. Accuracy alone is not adequate: shoreline patches are overwhelmingly 'not encroached' in any given year, so a trivial always-negative classifier would score high accuracy while being useless.
evaluation.validation_protocol: leave-one-lake-out is mandatory. Patches from the same lake share imaging conditions, shoreline geometry, and (if manually labelled) an annotator's judgement calls about that specific lake, so any split that is not lake-based leaks. With only 6 lakes this gives 6 folds, each one testing generalisation to an entire unseen lake -- a genuinely hard test given how different the 6 lakes are (e.g. Bellandur's extreme hyacinth cover versus Sankey Tank's small, clean 12.4 ha tank).
evaluation.leakage_risk: (1) Same-lake patches split across train and test (spatial autocorrelation) will inflate apparent performance; (2) the same physical shoreline location appearing in multiple years lets the model memorise a lake's specific shoreline shape and colour rather than learning a general encroachment cue (temporal leakage); (3) if labels are derived from the same MNDWI/NDVI/OSM rule used as the classical baseline, any measured 'improvement' of the CNN over that baseline is circular by construction, since the CNN is being scored on how well it reproduces its own training signal.
evaluation.uncertainty_reporting: None by default -- a plain CNN classifier produces a bare point-estimate probability per patch. Given only 6 independent lakes and zero true ground truth, a bootstrap band across lakes (resampling which lakes are held out) or a conformal-prediction wrapper (item C7) should accompany any reported F1/AUC before it is shown to a panel.
evaluation.augmentation_honesty_risk: Standard geometric image augmentation (flips, rotations, small photometric jitter) applied to the manually labelled patches is low-risk and should be disclosed as ordinary data multiplication of real observations, not additional real-world evidence. Higher risk if class-imbalance correction is done via feature-space oversampling (e.g. SMOTE) on the minority 'encroached' class: synthetic minority patches only interpolate between a handful of hand-labelled examples and could smooth over exactly the ambiguity (is this desilting, hyacinth, or true encroachment?) that the manual labelling protocol was supposed to resolve. If used, this must be disclosed explicitly and its effect on reported metrics checked with and without the synthetic samples.

evidence.published_performance: This is a bespoke, task-specific baseline rather than a named benchmark method, so there is no single number to cite for 'CNN patch classifier for lake encroachment.' Related precedents: patch/image-level (rather than pixel-level) labels have been shown to be a workable, cheaper supervision signal for remote-sensing change detection generally (MS-Former, arXiv 2311.09726, weakly supervised change detection with patch-level annotations) [verify], and CNN-based coastline/shoreline classification has been demonstrated at very-high-resolution aerial/coastal imagery (e.g. Sobel-edge-loss U-Net variants, ScienceDirect 2022, DOI referenced in that paper) [verify] -- but none of this is at 20 m resolution, none targets 'encroachment' semantics, and none is India- or Bengaluru-specific. No comparable published accuracy figure for this exact task exists to quote; reporting 'no established benchmark' is the honest position rather than borrowing an unrelated number.
evidence.study_area_of_that_work: MS-Former and comparable weakly-supervised change-detection work use standard VHR change-detection benchmarks (LEVIR-CD-class datasets, sub-2 m/px); coastline-CNN work uses VHR aerial/coastal imagery internationally (US coastlines, Coast Train dataset). None of this is at lake/wetland scale, none is at 20 m, and none is in India.
evidence.applies_to_indian_urban_lakes: No published instance was found of a CNN patch classifier applied to encroachment detection on Bengaluru or any Indian urban lake using Sentinel-2 imagery. Building this would be a novel, if methodologically modest, application for this specific domain.
evidence.evidence_recency: 2022-2024 for the closest generic precedents (weakly-supervised patch-level change detection, coastline CNN work); no dedicated evidence newer or more specific exists for this exact task on this exact data.
evidence.primary_sources: MS-Former (weakly supervised patch-level change detection): https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.09726 ; general sample-efficient change-detection survey: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.02835 ; coastline detection CNN precedent: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0034425722001584 ; macrophyte cross-check for Bellandur/Varthur: DOI 10.3390/rs12223843 ; project's own current classical baseline (Xu 2006 MNDWI) is the comparison point this CNN must beat, per project_constraints.current_method.

risk.failure_modes: The dominant failure mode is the label source, not the architecture: labels are either circular (derived from the same MNDWI/NDVI rule the CNN is meant to outperform) or expensive and subjective (manual annotation, with likely low inter-annotator agreement on exactly the two hardest cases in this project -- a desilted lakebed and a hyacinth mat). With only 6 lakes, leave-one-lake-out testing is likely to show unstable, low, or highly variable performance because 5 training lakes cannot represent the shoreline diversity needed to generalise to a 6th, very different lake. The mismatch between patch size (needed for spatial context) and the narrow legal buffer (30-75 m, 1.5-4 pixels wide) means the model is effectively classifying a much wider, blurrier strip of land than the buffer it is meant to speak to.
risk.panel_defensibility: The first and most damaging question a panel will ask is 'who labelled encroached versus not, and how do you know they were right?' There is no way to answer this honestly without naming the exact protocol: manual visual judgement against historical high-resolution imagery, with a stated inter-annotator agreement figure (Cohen's kappa), and an explicit acknowledgement that 'encroached' here means 'judged as converted to built-up/cultivated land by an untrained-in-law student annotator,' not a confirmed legal encroachment. If the labels instead come from the MNDWI/NDVI rule, the panel will correctly observe that the CNN cannot be shown to beat the very rule that generated its training signal, which undercuts the entire point of building it. This item is the honesty test-case for the whole project, and the note's instruction to 'state the label source honestly' should be treated as the headline of the writeup, not a footnote.
risk.honest_expectation: As a genuine deep-learning baseline requiring real, if modest, manual labelling effort, this CNN will most plausibly perform roughly on par with, not decisively better than, the classical MNDWI/Random Forest baseline, given only a few hundred hand-labelled patches drawn from just 6 lakes. That is itself a fair, reportable outcome: the value of building it is having an honestly labelled, documented dataset and a fair comparison point to test the 'deep learning beats classical rules' claim, not an expectation of a large accuracy jump. A null result here (CNN ties or trails the classical baseline) is entirely plausible and should be reported as such rather than reframed as a success.

verdict.recommended_rank: adopt-if-time -- this is the standard deep baseline the guide will expect a comparison against, and it is cheap to build once labels exist, but the student-days budget must be allocated to labelling (the real cost) rather than modelling, and the result should be reported as a fair comparison, not inflated.
verdict.one_line_for_the_guide: We built a CNN patch classifier on shoreline patches using labels from manual visual inspection of historical high-resolution imagery (roughly 6-10 student-days, mostly labelling), validated it lake-by-lake since patches within a lake are not independent, and it performed comparably to -- not clearly better than -- the classical MNDWI/Random Forest baseline it was meant to beat, which we report as an honest, if unglamorous, finding.
